report.source_text: On examination the visual acuity was noted to be 6/36 left eye and 6/9 right eye. He had bilateral medial lower lid ectropion accounting for the epiphora. Anterior segment examination and intraocular pressures were normal. Posterior segment examination revealed marked retinal ischaemia present in the posterior pole and macular region of both eyes. Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) confirmed an ischaemic retina. There were no signs of neovascularization (see figure 2). The distribution of the retinal changes with severe ischaemic changes in the posterior retina more than in the anterior retina, the relative lack of microaneurysms compared to the high numbers of cotton wool spots and blot haemorrhages and the rapid nature in which the retinopathy developed made the diagnosis of radiation retinopathy likely. Additionally the temporal onset of the retinopathy in relation to the radiotherapy (1 year post treatment) and the dose delivered further supported this diagnosis.

report.source_text: Over the next four months the vision in both eyes rapidly deteriorated to 3/60 left eye and 1/60 right eye. Clinical examination revealed bilateral vitreous haemorrhage. FFA confirmed bilateral disc neovascularisation and evidence of a grossly ischaemic retina with little residual viable retina (see figure 3). Bilateral pan retinal photocoagulation was considered to be appropriate treatment at this stage as it was thought that the minimal remaining, highly ischaemic, retina close to the arcades may be responsible for the disc neovascularisation. The total area of treatment in RE was 2595 mm2 and in the LE 1825 mm2.

report.source_text: At review in September 2006 the visual acuities were counting fingers in the RE and 6/60 aided in the LE. The retinopathy is stable.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 55-year-old male with prior nasal squamous cell carcinoma treated with radiotherapy presented with epiphora and decreased visual acuity. Examination showed bilateral medial lower lid ectropion, normal anterior segment and intraocular pressures, but marked retinal ischemia in both eyes. Fluorescein angiography demonstrated extensive ischemic retina without neovascularization one year post-radiotherapy, consistent with radiation retinopathy. Over four months, visual acuity rapidly worsened, and bilateral vitreous hemorrhage and disc neovascularisation developed. Pan retinal photocoagulation was performed. At subsequent follow-up, visual acuity was counting fingers in the right eye and 6/60 in the left eye, with stable retinopathy.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Posterior segment examination revealed marked retinal ischemia in both eyes.
Fluorescein angiography showed ischemic retina with no neovascularisation, consistent with radiation retinopathy, one year after radiotherapy.
Over four months vision deteriorated with vitreous hemorrhage and disc neovascularisation requiring bilateral pan retinal photocoagulation.
Follow-up showed stable retinopathy with reduced visual acuity after treatment.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: No diabetic retinal disease documented in diabetic retinal check 1 year prior; rapid progression and retinal ischemia pattern more consistent with radiation retinopathy.

remaining_uncertainties: No available OCT imaging to characterize retinal structural changes.
Limited direct exclusion of other ischemic retinopathies in late course documented.
